triage.name: Diabetes and Pregnancy
triage.reason: Pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes is a manageable case: glycemic history, monitoring and maternal-fetal risk assessment.

demographics: Occurs in pregnant women of any race or ethnicity
Higher rates of gestational diabetes in African American, Hispanic/Latina, American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander women
Pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes is increasingly common in pregnancy as rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes rise in women of childbearing age

risk_factors.text: Family history of diabetes in a first-degree relative
Gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy
Previous infant weighing 9 pounds (4 kg) or more

comorbidities: Prior pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia or macrosomia
family_history: Type 2 diabetes in a parent or sibling
Gestational diabetes in a mother or sister

chief_complaints.text: I'm pregnant and my blood sugar has been high
I'm thirstier than usual and peeing all the time
I feel tired all the time
My doctor said my glucose screening test was abnormal

hpi.onset: Often gradual and detected on routine prenatal screening; women with pre-existing diabetes may notice worsening glucose control as pregnancy progresses
hpi.duration: Gestational diabetes is usually diagnosed at 24–28 weeks; pre-existing diabetes is present before conception
hpi.progression: Insulin resistance rises through the second and third trimesters, so glucose levels and medication needs tend to increase until near term
hpi.severity: Often asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they are mild
hpi.timing: Symptoms, if any, are persistent rather than episodic
pertinent_negatives: Leakage of fluid from the vagina

negatives: Numbness or tingling in hands or feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Higher baseline insulin resistance means glucose levels rise earlier and higher, and more women need medication rather than diet alone.
Women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes often have symptoms of hyperglycemia and known complications before pregnancy, and their insulin requirements change markedly through pregnancy.
Pregnancy over age 35 carries higher baseline risk of gestational diabetes and hypertensive complications, and symptoms may be attributed to age rather than hyperglycemia.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; uterine size consistent with dates
general.moderate: Well-appearing but tired; may appear overweight or obese; no acute distress
general.severe: Ill-appearing with signs of dehydration from hyperglycemia (dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor) or hypertensive urgency
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, signs of severe dehydration, Kussmaul respirations, or seizures from severe preeclampsia/eclampsia

findings.maneuver: Measure fundal height with a tape from the pubic symphysis to the top of the fundus
findings.finding: Fundal height greater than expected for gestational age, suggesting macrosomia or polyhydramnios

findings.maneuver: Auscultate fetal heart tones with a Doppler or fetoscope
findings.finding: Fetal heart tones present and regular in the expected range (110–160/min)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the uterus for tenderness and assess uterine tone
findings.finding: Uterine tenderness or hypertonicity suggesting abruption or preterm labor

findings.maneuver: Press the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area for 5 seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and hands for swelling
findings.finding: Swelling of the face or hands suggesting preeclampsia

findings.maneuver: Test deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis, patella and Achilles
findings.finding: Hyperreflexia or clonus suggesting preeclampsia with severe features
Diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, or proliferative changes)

findings.maneuver: Inspect skin folds, feet and perineum
findings.finding: Candidal intertrigo, vulvovaginitis, or skin infections associated with hyperglycemia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the feet and test protective sensation with a 10-g monofilament
findings.finding: Diabetic neuropathy with loss of protective sensation or foot ulcers
Clear to auscultation bilaterally without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs or gallops; normal peripheral pulses

findings.maneuver: Assess cranial nerves, strength and sensation
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficits, no severe headache or visual changes

labs.caveat: Fasting plasma glucose. In pregnancy, fasting ≥92 mg/dL meets criteria for gestational diabetes; values ≥126 mg/dL suggest overt pre-existing diabetes.

Used to assess pre-pregnancy and early-pregnancy glycemic control; A1c ≥6.5% suggests pre-existing diabetes. A1c is less reliable in later pregnancy due to hemodilution and increased red cell turnover.
Glucosuria reflects glucose above the renal threshold; can be positive in pregnancy even with normal glucose due to increased GFR.
Ketones suggest inadequate carbohydrate intake, starvation ketosis, or diabetic ketoacidosis; important to assess in type 1 diabetes.
Proteinuria may indicate preeclampsia or diabetic nephropathy; requires quantification with protein/creatinine ratio.
Creatinine normally falls in pregnancy due to increased GFR; a value ≥0.8 mg/dL may indicate renal impairment.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from diabetic ketoacidosis.
Hypokalemia can occur with insulin treatment and osmotic diuresis in diabetic ketoacidosis.
Confirms pregnancy and establishes gestational age; essential before initiating any diabetes management plan.
Thyroid dysfunction is more common in women with type 1 diabetes and can affect pregnancy outcomes.

imaging.preferred_when: 18–22 weeks gestation for detailed anatomy; earlier for dating and viability

findings.text: Fetal biometry consistent with dates or showing macrosomia (estimated fetal weight >90th percentile)
Fetal cardiac, neural tube, or other structural anomalies

imaging.preferred_when: Women with pre-existing diabetes and poor glycemic control (A1c >6.5%) or elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein

findings.text: Congenital heart defects (ventricular septal defect, transposition of great arteries, truncus arteriosus)

imaging.preferred_when: Third trimester, especially with pre-existing diabetes or poor control
Suspected fetal growth restriction or maternal vascular disease

findings.text: Normal forward flow with low resistance
Increased resistance or absent/reversed end-diastolic flow

imaging.preferred_when: All women with pre-existing diabetes at first prenatal visit and each trimester

findings.text: Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates)
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy or macular edema

initial.why: Fasting glucose to screen for or diagnose diabetes in pregnancy
Assesses pre-pregnancy and early-pregnancy glycemic control; identifies pre-existing diabetes
Baseline hemoglobin, platelets; anemia is common in pregnancy
Baseline renal function, electrolytes, and glucose
Screens for glucosuria, ketonuria, proteinuria, and urinary infection
Thyroid dysfunction is more common in type 1 diabetes and affects pregnancy
Baseline assessment for diabetic retinopathy, which can worsen in pregnancy

confirmatory.why: Diagnostic test for gestational diabetes; fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL meets criteria
Screening test; if ≥130–140 mg/dL, proceed to diagnostic OGTT

supporting.why: Detects congenital heart defects associated with poor glycemic control
supporting.only_if: pre-existing diabetes with A1c >6.5% or abnormal anatomy survey

supporting.why: Monitors for macrosomia and growth restriction
Assesses fetal well-being in growth restriction
Assesses renal function; elevated creatinine may indicate nephropathy

not_indicated.why: Not useful for diagnosing preeclampsia or diabetes in pregnancy; elevated in normal pregnancy
Not routinely needed unless diabetic ketoacidosis or sepsis is suspected

not_indicated.test: ct abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Avoid ionizing radiation in pregnancy unless a life-threatening condition requires it
Not indicated for diabetes in pregnancy

decision_points: Screen for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks in all pregnant women; screen early if high risk
Diagnose gestational diabetes with 75 g OGTT using IADPSG criteria: fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL
In pre-existing diabetes, optimize A1c before conception and monitor closely during pregnancy
Assess for preeclampsia if new hypertension or proteinuria develops
Perform retinal exam each trimester in pre-existing diabetes

criteria.name: Gestational diabetes diagnostic criteria (IADPSG/ADA)
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is made if any one of the following thresholds is met or exceeded on a 75 g 2-hour OGTT: fasting plasma glucose 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL.

criteria.name: Overt diabetes in pregnancy
criteria.summary: Diagnosed when fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, A1c ≥6.5%, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms.
items: Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms

differential.name: Preeclampsia
differential.why_considered: Both conditions occur in pregnancy and share risk factors such as obesity, chronic hypertension and pre-existing diabetes; new hypertension or proteinuria in a pregnant woman with diabetes raises concern.
differential.trigger: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria, headache, visual changes, or right upper quadrant pain

history: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Rapid swelling of face and hands
exam: Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg or higher on two occasions
labs: Proteinuria on urine protein/creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection
imaging: Fetal growth restriction or oligohydramnios on ultrasound
Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler in severe disease

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Pregnancy accelerates ketosis and insulin resistance, so women with type 1 diabetes can present with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain that mimic routine pregnancy complaints.
differential.trigger: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, or fruity breath odor in a pregnant woman with diabetes

history: Polydipsia and polyuria out of proportion to pregnancy
Rapid onset of vomiting and abdominal pain

differential.name: Hyperemesis gravidarum
differential.why_considered: Persistent nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy can cause dehydration, ketonuria and starvation ketosis that resemble poorly controlled diabetes.

history: Vomiting beginning in the first trimester
labs: Urine ketones from starvation rather than hyperglycemia

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Pregnant women with diabetes have more frequent urinary infections, and both conditions can cause urinary frequency and malaise.

labs: Positive urine leukocyte esterase and nitrites
Glucose may be normal or elevated

differential.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Overt diabetes may first be recognized during pregnancy, and it shares obesity, family history and glucosuria with gestational diabetes.

differential.name: Chronic hypertension
differential.why_considered: Frequently coexists with diabetes in pregnancy and can be confused with preeclampsia when blood pressure rises.

history: Hypertension diagnosed before pregnancy or before 20 weeks
exam: Elevated blood pressure without facial or hand edema

differential.name: Fetal macrosomia from other causes
differential.why_considered: A larger-than-dates uterus can reflect macrosomia from diabetes but also from constitutional factors or post-term pregnancy.

imaging: Estimated fetal weight above the 90th percentile with normal amniotic fluid

severity.mild: Gestational diabetes or well-controlled pre-existing diabetes managed with diet and activity alone; fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL and normal fetal growth.
severity.moderate: Diabetes requiring medication (insulin or an oral agent) with glucose near target; no maternal vascular complications and normal fetal growth.
severity.severe: Poorly controlled diabetes with A1c above 7%, macrosomia or polyhydramnios, or worsening retinopathy or nephropathy.
severity.critical: Diabetic ketoacidosis, severe preeclampsia or eclampsia, or diabetic coma with fetal compromise.

red_flags.finding: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing or fruity breath
red_flags.meaning: Diabetic ketoacidosis; a maternal and fetal emergency requiring immediate treatment

red_flags.finding: Blood pressure 160/110 mmHg or higher, severe headache, visual changes or right upper quadrant pain
red_flags.meaning: Preeclampsia with severe features; risk of seizure, stroke and placental abruption

red_flags.finding: Decreased fetal movement or abnormal fetal heart tracing
red_flags.meaning: Fetal compromise; needs urgent obstetric evaluation
Placental abruption or other obstetric emergency

red_flags.finding: Leakage of fluid or regular painful contractions before term
red_flags.meaning: Preterm labor, which is more common with diabetes

red_flags.finding: Severe hypoglycemia with confusion or loss of consciousness
red_flags.meaning: Tight glycemic control in pregnancy increases hypoglycemia risk, especially in type 1 diabetes

complications.name: Macrosomia
clues: Estimated fetal weight above the 90th percentile on ultrasound

complications.name: Congenital birth defects
clues: Cardiac, neural tube or renal anomalies on anatomy ultrasound

complications.name: Neonatal hypoglycemia
clues: Jitteriness or poor feeding after birth

complications.name: Shoulder dystocia and birth trauma
clues: Neonatal clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury

special_populations.differences: This is the defining population; insulin resistance rises through the second and third trimesters, so medication needs increase until near term and then fall sharply after delivery.
Higher baseline insulin resistance means glucose rises earlier and higher, and more women need medication rather than diet alone.
Women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes need pre-conception planning, tighter targets and monitoring for retinopathy, nephropathy and hypoglycemia.
Pregnancy over age 35 carries higher baseline risk of gestational diabetes and hypertensive complications.
Pre-existing nephropathy increases the risk of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction, and creatinine must be interpreted against the lower pregnancy reference range.
Pregnancy in adolescents with diabetes is uncommon but carries higher risks of preterm birth and poor glycemic control because of social and care-access barriers.

key_questions.question: When was your last menstrual period, and how far along are you?
key_questions.looking_for: Gestational age, which determines whether screening at 24–28 weeks is due and how insulin resistance is expected to change

key_questions.question: Did you have diabetes before this pregnancy, or was it first found during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes versus gestational diabetes; changes the whole management plan

key_questions.question: What was your blood sugar control like before you became pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pre-conception A1c and glucose levels; poor early control raises the risk of birth defects

key_questions.question: Have you been thirstier than usual or urinating more often?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild hyperglycemic symptoms; often absent in gestational diabetes

key_questions.question: Have you had blurred vision, floaters, or any change in your eyesight?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetic retinopathy, which can worsen during pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had swelling of your face or hands, headaches, or visual spots?
key_questions.looking_for: Preeclampsia, which is more common with diabetes in pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any right upper quadrant or severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: HELLP syndrome, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, or diabetic ketoacidosis

key_questions.question: Have you felt the baby move normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Decreased fetal movement, which requires urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you had any vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, or regular contractions?
key_questions.looking_for: Placental abruption, preterm labor, or rupture of membranes

key_questions.question: What diabetes medicines are you taking, and have you needed to change the doses?
key_questions.looking_for: Insulin regimen and dose changes; some oral agents are not used in pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had gestational diabetes, a large baby, or preeclampsia in a past pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Strong risk factors for gestational diabetes and recurrence

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with type 2 diabetes, a major risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had frequent vaginal or urinary infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent candidal or urinary infections associated with hyperglycemia

key_questions.question: Do you have any numbness, tingling, or sores on your feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetic neuropathy or foot ulcers in pre-existing diabetes

reasoning_points: Pregnancy with hyperglycemia, either pre-existing diabetes or glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy
Gestational diabetes is usually asymptomatic and found on routine screening at 24–28 weeks, or earlier if high risk
Diagnosis rests on a 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test using IADPSG/ADA thresholds: fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL
Overt or pre-existing diabetes is suggested by fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, A1c ≥6.5%, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms
Insulin resistance rises through the second and third trimesters, so glucose levels and medication needs increase until near term
Maternal risks include preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, worsening retinopathy and nephropathy, and later type 2 diabetes
Fetal and neonatal risks include macrosomia, congenital birth defects with poor early control, neonatal hypoglycemia, and stillbirth
Preeclampsia, diabetic ketoacidosis, and fetal compromise must be excluded because they change management urgently

easy: Routine prenatal visit at 24–28 weeks with an abnormal 50 g glucose challenge test
No symptoms, normal examination, normal fetal growth
Classic risk factors such as obesity and a family history of diabetes
Diagnosis confirmed on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
medium: Pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes with changing insulin requirements through pregnancy
Fundal height greater than dates suggesting macrosomia or polyhydramnios
Mild hyperglycemic symptoms attributed to normal pregnancy
Coexisting chronic hypertension raising concern for preeclampsia
hard: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain in a woman with type 1 diabetes suggesting diabetic ketoacidosis
New hypertension with headache or visual changes suggesting preeclampsia with severe features
Decreased fetal movement or an abnormal fetal heart tracing requiring urgent obstetric evaluation
Pregnancy in an adolescent or a woman with limited prenatal care and poor glycemic control
Pre-existing nephropathy with a creatinine that looks normal but is elevated for pregnancy
